summary: A schooling, brackish-water-loving panfish common in estuaries, tidal headponds, and barrier-beach ponds across NB, NS, and PEI. Bag limits have recently been tightened in both NS and PEI, so check current numbers before keeping a big cooler-full.

sections.heading: Know the Fish
sections.body_md: White perch (*Morone americana*) are a small, silvery, deep-bodied member of the temperate bass family (related to striped bass, not to yellow perch despite the name) — no stripes, no dark bars, just a uniform silver-to-olive body and two connected dorsal fins. Most run 7-11 inches. They're a schooling species that tolerates a wide salinity range, which is why they thrive in estuaries, river mouths, and the brackish barrier-beach ponds common along the PEI and NB coastlines, as well as in freshwater headponds well upriver.

sources.label: Nova Scotia Invasive Species Council, Chain Pickerel (native-alternative species reference)

sections.heading: Where to Find Them
sections.body_md:
**New Brunswick:** anglers report good white perch fishing at the **Hampton Lighthouse River Centre** area on the Kennebecasis, the **Mactaquac headpond** on the Saint John River, **Maquapit Lake**, and **Wauklehegan Lake**.

**PEI:** white perch are common in the island's estuaries and brackish **barrier-beach ponds**, including documented catches in the **Johnstons River** and **Desroches Pond** systems, and in the Morell River system alongside brook trout.

**Nova Scotia:** found in tidal rivers and estuaries province-wide wherever brackish, slow-current water exists — check local river mouths and headponds.

sources.label: New Brunswick Fishing Forum, White Perch Fishing

sections.heading: When to Go
sections.body_md: White perch move into shallower, warmer water to spawn in spring, which is when they're easiest to find and catch in numbers close to shore. They remain a solid summer-through-fall target in estuaries and headponds, and in PEI in particular, ice fishing for perch through the winter has grown into its own dedicated fishery on brackish ponds where ice forms reliably.

sources.label: CBC News, Ice fishing for perch could be a thing on P.E.I.

sections.heading: Gear
sections.body_md:
| Item | Recommendation |
|---|---|
| Rod | Light spinning rod, 6-7 ft, 4-8 lb line — white perch fight modestly and light gear makes it fun. |
| Terminal tackle | Small jigs, spinners, or a simple bobber-and-worm/minnow rig. |
| Bait | Worms, small minnows, or small strips of cut bait work well in brackish water. |
| Ice gear | Same small jigs/teardrops used for yellow perch, tipped with a waxworm or minnow head. |

sections.heading: Technique
sections.body_md:
1. Fish river mouths, headpond current seams, and pond inlets where fresh and brackish water mix — perch stack up at these transition zones.
2. Once you find a school, stay on it — white perch bite fast and often in numbers, similar to yellow perch.
3. A simple bobber rig with a small piece of worm or a small jig worked slowly near bottom will out-produce more complicated presentations for this species.
4. In headponds like Mactaquac, fish the slower, deeper water along the margins of the main current rather than in the fastest flow.

sections.heading: Conservation & Consumption Notes
sections.body_md: White perch are good, mild table fish, but bag limits have been trending down across the region as fisheries managers keep an eye on local population pressure — Nova Scotia's current Anglers' Handbook lists the white perch bag limit reduced to **10 fish**, and PEI's daily limit was cut from a historical 100 fish down to **25 fish** in recent regulation summaries. Fish conservatively even where an older, higher number might still be floating around online — always check the current-year regulations summary for your province before keeping a full cooler.

variants.name: Juvenile Striped Bass
variants.how_to_tell: This is the single most important ID check in this guide. Striped bass carry 7-8 dark, continuous horizontal stripes running the length of the body — white perch have none at all, just a uniform silvery-to-olive flank. If stripes aren't obvious, check the tongue: striped bass have two distinct tooth patches on the back of the tongue (feel for two rough spots running your finger down the centerline), while white perch have none. Body shape backs this up too — striped bass are slender and torpedo-shaped (depth less than about a third of body length), while white perch are noticeably deeper-bodied for their size. Striped bass also have two dorsal fins that are clearly separated with a gap between them; a white perch's two dorsal fins are close together, nearly touching.
variants.where_found: Juvenile striped bass use the exact same brackish estuary and headpond water white perch do across all three provinces — anywhere you catch white perch, a small striper is a realistic catch too, especially near river mouths that connect to known striped bass spawning rivers like the Miramichi.
variants.notes: This is a legally serious mix-up. Striped bass have a minimum retainable size in all three provinces, and undersized striped bass must be released — keeping one because it was mistaken for a white perch is an offence. Check stripes and the tongue on every fish before it goes in the cooler, not just the ones that look obviously different.

variants.name: Yellow Perch
variants.how_to_tell: Yellow perch are a true perch (family Percidae), not a bass, and look it: a golden-yellow body with 6-8 sharp, dark vertical bars, versus a white perch's plain silvery-olive flank with no bars or stripes at all. Yellow perch also have a triangular pelvic fin angled out at roughly 45 degrees, while a white perch's pelvic fin points straight down and widens toward the tip.
variants.where_found: Both species share freshwater headponds and lake systems, including stretches of the Saint John River system — yellow perch lean more toward fully fresh water, white perch tolerate brackish water further downstream.
variants.notes: No shared retention concern, but yellow perch cannot legally be used as bait anywhere in NB, a rule that does not apply to white perch — worth knowing if you're catching incidental fish to use as bait for something else.
